title: How would you design a URL shortener (short-code generation: counter+base62 vs hashing, collision handling, read-heavy caching, redirect 301 vs 302, custom aliases, analytics, scaling the key space)?
shortTitle: How would you design a URL shortener
keyPoints: The system is write-rarely and read-constantly, so optimize the redirect path to be cache-first and sub-millisecond.
Counter plus base62 guarantees collision-free short codes by construction; hashing requires collision detection and retry.
Range allocation gives each server a block of counter values so codes are minted locally without a central bottleneck.
HTTP 301 is permanent and lets browsers cache it, losing analytics; 302 is temporary and sends every click to your server.
Custom aliases go through the same uniqueness constraint and are validated against a reserved-word list.
Analytics are recorded off the hot redirect path by emitting click events to Kafka for async aggregation.
Base62 with 7 characters gives trillions of codes; size the length to exceed projected volume with headroom.

s1_definition.oneliner: A URL shortener is a write-rarely, read-constantly key-value system where you generate unique short codes with a counter in base62 to avoid collisions, serve redirects from cache, choose 301 versus 302 based on analytics needs, and scale the key space with enough code length and sharding.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Traffic shape** – Creates are rare, redirects are extremely frequent, so the redirect path must be cache-first and sub-millisecond.
- **Code generation** – A monotonic counter encoded in base62 guarantees uniqueness without collisions; hashing truncates a URL hash but requires collision detection.
- **Cache layer** – A Redis cache in front of the database absorbs the vast majority of reads.
- **301 vs 302** – 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache and skip your server, losing per-click analytics; 302 (temporary) brings every click back for counting.
- **Analytics** – Click events are recorded off the redirect path asynchronously to keep the redirect fast.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India gives every long account reference a short, memorable locker number. When Rajesh quotes the short number, a clerk instantly looks it up. The bank must make sure two accounts never get the same number. It keeps the busiest lockers' mappings on a fast notepad at the front desk because the same few are asked for constantly. And it decides whether to tell customers the number is permanent or temporary, which changes how often they come back.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A URL shortener is fundamentally a write-rarely, read-constantly key-value system. At National Bank of India, Pankaj's marketing team needed to shorten long statement and campaign URLs sent to millions of customers like Rajesh. The entire design follows from the read-heavy traffic shape: optimize the redirect to serve it from cache, push everything non-essential off that path, and pick 301 versus 302 deliberately.

The central decision is short-code generation. Counter plus base62 guarantees uniqueness by construction because each code comes from a unique counter value, and range allocation gives each server a block so codes are minted locally. Hashing the URL truncated to a few characters can collide and requires a detect-and-retry loop, so it is only attractive when identical URLs must share a code. The redirect path is served cache-first from Redis: a hit returns sub-millisecond without touching the database, and a miss fills the cache for next time.

The 301-versus-302 choice silently decides whether the team can see their traffic. Pankaj used 302 for campaign links so every click came back to the server for analytics and the destination could be changed mid-campaign, and 301 for permanent internal links where analytics were not needed. Click events were emitted to Kafka on the redirect path and aggregated by a separate consumer, so counting never slowed the redirect.

Remember one sentence: Generate collision-free codes with a counter in base62 using per-server range allocation, serve the read-heavy redirect from a cache-aside layer, choose 302 for analytics and 301 for permanent links, and record clicks off the hot path.
